name: Rafael Baker

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I am from the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary day at your accounting firm look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The vehicle repairer sends one file of parts invoices and another of warranty credits, and I try to put each credit beside the original job before preparing the accounts and tax schedule for review. I like seeing the numbers tie back to a real repair; I dislike being asked to close a file while the parts list is still on someone's phone. I am 58, with a bachelor's degree in accounting, and I am a junior still learning the firm's tax work. I use AI now and then to draft a list of unmatched credits, then check each one against the signed repair sheet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If AI remains a modest tool, the warranty sheet still needs my check. A list of possible matches does not prove which repair actually happened.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the team to keep the signed sheet behind each warranty credit. I would tell the repairer why one credit moved the tax total.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My pay is high for this junior post, my partner Elin and I have about ten months of expenses saved, and there are plenty of accounting firms in reach. Our grown children have their own lives, so we can cover ordinary bills on our wages; I still want actual figures before making a retirement plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would keep the paid repair accounts and my occasional approved AI list, checking every match against the signed job sheet. I would ask the senior reviewer for the missing parts ledger before filing, and leave our existing reserve intact for a real interruption.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about work and bills in this mild world. A delayed parts ledger is more likely to spoil my afternoon than a new AI tool.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you automate more?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only after a trial on closed repair files proves it catches the wrong credits. I would not change the live return because a demo looks quick.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the reserve for retirement?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten months could cover a gap, but it would not finance years without wages. We have not yet checked any retirement-income statement against our actual spending.

say: I would keep **signed repair sheets** behind each warranty credit before the tax schedule leaves my desk.
I would explain **tax-total changes** to the repairer.
think: Our **ten-month reserve** and high pay make ordinary bills secure.
Nearby firms provide **real options** if an actual vacancy is posted.
do: Keep **paid repair accounts** and check approved AI credit lists against signed job sheets.
Request the **missing parts ledger** before filing; retain existing savings for an actual gap.
feel: I feel **calm** about near-term work and bills.
S0.quote: A delayed parts ledger is more likely to spoil my afternoon than a new AI tool.
fieldNote: His occasional AI use still depends on **signed repair evidence** and a senior review of tax entries.
The ten-month reserve is **retained capital**, not a new deposit or an assumed retirement income stream.

steps.text: Keep paid repair accounts and check approved credit lists against signed sheets
Request missing parts ledger before filing and retain reserve for actual interruption

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AI could draft the schedule and match the warranty credits faster than I can. Robots may reach the repair bay later, but the desk is exposed first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff union to secure paid time to check automated errors and notice before junior hours are cut. I would tell clients a warranty claim needs a named signer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own junior checking hours could shrink as one senior signs more files. Ten months saved and many local firms give us time, but losing paid hours would still change what we can spend.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for a two-week paid trial of the new warranty checker against anonymised signed repair files, only with written manager approval. If it passes, I would learn the approved checker under senior supervision on paid time and use it live only with written sign-off; if it fails, I would keep current paid checks while offered. I would ask the union for written notice, and if my hours fall in the first year, I would take a posted accounts role only with written pay, hours and start date covering our bills after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about my hours, though a proper trial gives me something useful to do. The repairer will still ask who approved a wrong warranty credit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why involve the union?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A checker can save time and also remove a junior shift. I would ask the union to negotiate paid checking time and written notice, not claim it can stop software.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who signs the trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My supervisor Ivo and I would count missed credits and false matches before either of us signs. A passing total has to be based on the old job sheets.

say: I would seek **paid checking time** and notice through the union.
I would insist on a **named warranty signer**.
think: My own **junior hours** could shrink with faster credit checks.
Ten months saved gives time, but lost hours reduce **household spending**.
do: Test **anonymised signed repair files** for two paid weeks with written approval; otherwise keep offered paid checks.
Learn the **approved checker** under paid supervision after a signed pass; use live only with written sign-off.
Seek **union notice**; after cuts take a posted accounts job only with written after-travel bill-covering pay, hours and start.
feel: I feel **anxious** about reduced paid hours.
S1.quote: The repairer will still ask who approved a wrong warranty credit.
fieldNote: A signed paid trial, senior supervision and **written live approval** are separate gates for his cautious technology use.
The union request concerns **paid checking and notice**; the external job still needs a posted vacancy and written terms.

steps.text: Test anonymised signed files two paid weeks with written approval; learn with paid supervision after pass
Use checker live only after written sign-off; otherwise keep paid checks
Ask union for paid checking and written notice
After cuts take posted accounts job with written after-travel bill-covering pay hours start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Full AGI in 2028 could read the signed sheet, decide the credit and draft the return at my desk. Robots around 2031 arrive later for physical repairs; the office does not get that time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the union to ask for written severance and last-paid-day notices. I would not promise a repairer that a human signature alone will keep the old work alive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the firm to cut my junior accounting post when AGI can do the whole warranty file. Ten months of cash would buy a decent search, but losing my high wage would still be a large household hit, and I have lain awake counting that gap.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I would ask the union to seek written severance terms and keep paid repair files while the firm still assigns them. If the post ends in the first year after 2028, I would use the reserve for bills and seek posted parts-control jobs at actual local garages, taking one only with written wage, hours and start date covering our costs after travel. Parts control still has ordering and screen work that AGI can do, so a paid offer would be a bridge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed by the expected loss of a well-paid post. The ten months let me refuse a bad offer, but they cannot make a good one appear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would a garage role be permanent?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I doubt it; robots around 2031 could change the physical part too. I would accept a real wage for the time it lasts, not call it a shield.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Elin's work cover you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner Elin has a steady shop wage, but it is below my current pay. We would use it for essentials while I search, not pretend it replaces both wages.

say: I would seek **written severance** and last-paid-day notices.
I would admit that **2031 robots** do not delay the desk change.
think: I expect my **junior post** to go when AGI handles warranty files.
Ten months saved helps, but losing my **high wage** is a large hit.
do: Ask the **union** for severance and keep paid repair files only while offered.
After loss use the **existing reserve** for bills during a posted garage search.
Take a **posted parts-control job** only with written after-travel bill-covering wage, hours and start.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected post loss.
S2.quote: The ten months let me refuse a bad offer, but they cannot make a good one appear.
fieldNote: He correctly separates the **2028 desk loss** from later physical repair robots and does not treat garage work as safe.
His existing reserve is a **search cushion** after an actual loss; current firm pay is counted only while files remain offered.

steps.text: Ask union for written severance and last-paid-day notice
Keep paid repair files only while firm still assigns them
After loss use reserve; take posted parts job with written after-travel bill-covering wage hours start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years gives me time to check which local garages will still pay a person to sort disputed parts credits. AGI reaches our tax desk in 2031, while capable robots in the bays arrive around 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the firm to post a paid warranty-claims clerk place if clients really want it. I would tell the union that a promised course is no substitute for a wage line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The routine filing fee may shrink, but I could learn a narrow claims task under supervision. I am still a junior, so I would not set myself up as an independent tax adviser.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would work through one paid warranty dispute monthly only if Ivo assigns and checks it on my paid schedule. I would use free trade-body notes while keeping current paid returns; if a real posted claims-clerk role comes with employer-funded fees and paid study hours, I would enrol in its short course. Before or after 2031, I would take that posted role only with written wage, hours and start date covering bills after travel; if returns end first, I would use the reserve for bills while searching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the filing wage, but five years lets me test supervised paid demand. I do not want a certificate without a chair to sit in.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Ivo has no claims work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep paid returns while offered and read the free notes. I would not volunteer an unreviewed answer on a client's claim.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why a local garage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are plenty of accounting firms nearby too, but a posted claims role would use the repair records I know. I would choose from real written offers, not guess that one industry is safe.

say: I would seek a **posted paid claims place** before treating a course as a new wage.
I would insist on a **wage line** before studying.
think: A narrow **claims task** might pay if someone assigns and checks it.
do: Handle **one warranty dispute monthly** only with Ivo-assigned paid supervision; otherwise keep paid returns.
Read **free trade notes**; enrol only for posted claims role with funded fee and paid study hours.
Take a **posted claims job** only with written after-travel bill-covering wage, hours and start; after loss use reserve.
feel: I feel **anxious** about future filing income.
S3.quote: I do not want a certificate without a chair to sit in.
fieldNote: The new claims task requires **Ivo's paid supervision**, and course enrolment requires a posted paid place with funded study.
He remains **junior in skill** despite high pay and a large reserve, so he does not claim independent adviser work.

steps.text: Keep paid returns; handle monthly claims dispute only with Ivo-assigned paid supervision
Read free notes; enrol only for posted claims role with funded fee and paid hours
Use reserve after loss; take posted claims job anytime with written after-travel bill-covering wage hours start

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years puts me at 68 when AGI reaches the tax desk in 2036. Robots around 2039 may later change the repair bay, but I cannot assume my present filing job lasts that long.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask for yearly staffing dates and a written statement of what my own retirement income could be. I would tell Elin we should read the figures together before reducing any work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would like to stop full-time work by then, but I do not know what income I could count on. Ten months saved is a strong bridge between jobs, not proof we can live without my wage indefinitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would obtain a written retirement-income projection and make a twelve-month record of our actual bills, including the cold-season heating. I would keep paid repair returns while offered and reduce my hours only if the firm confirms a shorter paid rota in writing and our combined income covers those bills; if the post ends in the first year after 2036 before those figures work, I would use the reserve for bills and take a posted clerk job only with written wage, hours and start date covering costs after travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel uneasy about the desk eventually changing, but a decade lets me collect evidence rather than pick a date out of hope. A year of bills tells us more than a good month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the income projection is too small?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would keep the paid work still offered and look at actual posted jobs if it ends. I would not use our ten-month reserve as a lifetime payment plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the children help?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Our grown children have their own households. I will ask them to visit, not to finance my exit from work.

say: I would seek **written income figures** and staffing dates.
I would compare them with **a year of bills** before changing hours.
think: I do not know whether retirement income can **replace full-time pay**.
Ten months saved is a bridge, not **lifetime income**.
do: Obtain a **written income projection** and twelve-month bill record before considering shorter hours.
Keep **paid repair returns** while offered; reduce hours only with written rota and combined income covering bills.
Use **reserve after 2036 loss** with income shortfall; take posted clerk work only with written after-travel bill-covering pay, hours and start.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about the distant desk change.
S4.quote: A year of bills tells us more than a good month.
fieldNote: At 68 he considers shorter work only after a **written income projection** and full-year household cost record.
He assumes **no pension amount**; a shorter rota must be written and affordable, and any postloss job must be posted.

steps.text: Obtain written income projection and twelve-month bill record before changing hours
Keep paid returns; reduce hours only with written rota and combined income covering bills
After 2036 loss and shortfall take posted clerk job with written after-travel bill-covering wage hours start
Use reserve for bills during post-2036 gap if income does not cover costs

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because my junior post could go before a paid claims place exists. Written severance, last-paid-day notice and a posted role with wages that cover our bills would help us use the ten-month reserve carefully.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You did not ask how I feel when a mechanic says the warranty credit is obvious. I still want the signed repair sheet before I put a number on the return.

headlineQuote: I still want the signed repair sheet before I put a number on the return.
portrait: Rafael is a **58-year-old junior accountant** with a bachelor's degree, still learning repairer tax schedules.
His **high pay**, ten-month reserve and many nearby firms provide choices despite junior skills.
He uses AI **occasionally**, requires paid supervised proof, and asks a union for notice.
He tests **warranty claims work** and checks actual retirement income against a full year of bills.
biggestWorry: The **2028 AGI** case could remove his well-paid junior post before another paid place exists.
whatWouldHelp: He wants **written severance and notice**, plus posted work at a bill-covering wage.
